Hi Andrew / Maya — great question, glad you asked before procurement. Short answer up front then details:

- Metering: billed for tokens the server has already generated and committed (i.e., emitted to the stream). If the client disconnects after token N, you are billed for those N tokens. There is no automatic "rollback".
- Retries: if you retry the exact same request and it results in the server generating the same tokens again, those tokens are billed again unless you use our recommendation below (idempotency + resume).

Details + best practices:
- Token commitment: Redwood charges on tokens produced by the model runtime. For streaming, tokens are considered "committed" once they leave the runtime and are available to the client stream. Network disconnects do not implicitly cause credits to be returned.
- Idempotent requests: we provide request-id idempotency for the REST/streaming API. If you include the same request_id and the prior request completed server-side, our control plane can detect duplicates and avoid re-executing the same generation (no double-billing). This requires using the same idempotency key and not changing model parameters/prompt.
- Resume behavior: for long-running sessions we recommend a small server-side checkpoint token (conversation_id + kv_snapshot) so clients can reconnect and request resume from a last-confirmed token index. If you reconnect and request resume, we will continue from the checkpoint rather than regenerate already-committed tokens — that avoids double charges.
- Partial generations and timeouts: if a generation times out mid-run (e.g., max tokens or runtime limit), you are billed for produced tokens. If you restart a new generation that intentionally re-produces the same content, that will bill again unless you use idempotency/resume.

I've attached our hosted rate card baseline for quick reference and highlighted the streaming token price and recommended reserved-capacity rates for high-volume streaming customers.

If procurement needs formal language for the SOW/contract on "charged tokens" vs "delivered bytes" I can ask legal to include a short clause.

—Rishi
Rishi Malhotra

Hi Maya — quick reply with ballpark numbers and a proposed onboarding credit:

1) Onboarding credit: we typically offer a one-time "streaming stabilization" credit for new enterprise customers to cover unexpected partial-generation charge noise during the first 30 days. For Nimble Health we can offer up to $5k of credits applied to the first invoice (subject to contract). This is intended for network-induced partials and setup tuning.

2) Pricing example (hosted API baseline):
- Public baseline token price (hosted): $0.00006 / token (for the streaming-optimized model family listed on the rate card).
- 30M tokens at baseline = $1,800 / month.
- Volume tiers: 5% off at 10M+, 12% off at 25M+, 20% off at 100M+.

3) Dedicated / Reserved capacity (example):
- Reserved pool pricing: negotiated minimum commit that yields ~40–55% effective cost savings on token-equivalent throughput for heavy, steady streaming workloads. Exact numbers depend on concurrency, sequence lengths, and model family; we can run a workload estimate for Nimble.

I'll attach a draft mutual action plan and include a sample committed-tier quote for the 30M token example. Karthik — can you confirm the commit/discount bands we should propose for this account?
